tasks.title: Replace pg with a native PgProtocol client
tasks.body:
Closes EFF-880
Closes EFF-852
Closes EFF-858
Closes EFF-859
Closes EFF-870
Closes EFF-871
Closes EFF-872

Shared PR for all four native sql-pg client slices. Later slices push to this branch (`eff-854/pg-connection-startup`). Do not merge until slice 4 (PgClient switchover and `pg*` removal) is on the PR.

## Slice 1: connection startup

- `PgConnection.make` connects over TCP, Unix sockets, or a caller-supplied `Duplex`.
- Supports libpq URLs, optional TLS through `SSLRequest`, and trust, cleartext, MD5, or SCRAM-SHA-256 authentication.
- Resolves at `ReadyForQuery`; scope release sends `Terminate` and ends the socket after the frame flushes.
- Keeps `processId` public and the cancel secret private.

## Slice 2: unnamed extended query

- `query` and `queryValues` send `Parse` / `Bind` / `Describe` / `Execute` / `Sync` in one socket write and use binary parameters and result fields.
- One statement runs at a time per connection.
- JavaScript values infer OIDs; branded `PgTypes.Parameter` values override inference.
- `PgTypes.makeRegistry()` supplies isolated custom codecs and optional generic one-dimensional array codecs.
- Ordinary query errors drain through `ReadyForQuery`; parser failures, unexpected `COPY` messages, and protocol desync destroy the socket.
- Native results include command, row count, OID, fields, and object rows. `queryValues` preserves `RowDescription` order.

## Tests

- Live testcontainers coverage for startup, authentication failure, TLS refusal, SELECT, binary parameters, positional results, and connection recovery after a `23505` unique violation.
- In-process protocol tests for fragmented startup responses and connection edge cases.
- Unit coverage for URL validation, parameter branding, registry isolation, and custom array codecs.

## Performance

`benchmark/PgClient.ts` against one long-lived PostgreSQL container, client pinned to one CPU, alternating pairs,
median of the per-pair deltas. `main` still runs on `pg`.

| Workload | `main` | This branch | With `multiplex` |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| parameterized SELECT (1 row) | 22,589 q/s | 28,297 (+25%) | |
| generate_series (100 rows x 3 columns) | 1,082k rows/s | 1,662k (+54%) | |
| generate_series (100 rows x 20 columns) | 343k rows/s | 571k (+67%) | |
| transaction (1 INSERT) | 9,011 tx/s | 9,395 (+4%) | |
| 20 concurrent parameterized SELECTs | 77,741 q/s | 82,276 (+6%) | 123,309 (+61%) |

The changes:

- **Warmest connection first.** `Pool` released an item to the back of its availability list and borrowers took from
  the front, so a run of sequential borrows rotated over every connection the pool had opened and none was ever the
  hot one - a hundred sequential transactions landed on exactly ten backends, ten each, where node-postgres sent all
  hundred through one. A released item now goes to the front. Freshly acquired ones still go to the back, having no
  use behind them; under saturation the two orders agree.
- **`noDelay` on the session socket.** It had been set on the short-lived `CancelRequest` connection instead of the
  socket that carries every statement. Loopback hides this - a statement is one write and then a wait, so Nagle has
  nothing to hold anything behind - but across a virtual network it costs: on macOS through OrbStack the one-row query
  went from 4.6% behind `main` to 5.6% ahead.
- **Prepared transaction control.** `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK` and the savepoint pair went through
  `executeUnprepared`, so every transaction paid to parse them again. `SqlClient.MakeOptions` now takes
  `prepareTransactionControls`, which PostgreSQL sets and which is off for everyone else, since several databases
  refuse to prepare transaction control at all. Transactions were the one workload behind `main`, by 1.8%; they are
  now at parity.
- **Borrowed connections.** A statement that finishes with the effect that runs it opened a scope, leased a
  connection into it and closed it again. `SqlClient.MakeOptions` now takes an optional `borrower`, and `PgPool.use`
  lends a session for the duration of one effect through `Pool.use`. `stream`, transactions, and `reserve` keep the
  acquirer, whose lease outlives the effect that starts it; a driver that offers no borrower is unchanged. This is
  most of the concurrent workload's gain.
- **One permit per statement.** An ordinary statement entered both the ownership and the wire semaphore, but the wire
  permit is redundant once ownership is held: the other holders reach the session through ownership too, and a stream
  releases the wire before its pin. Pinned callers keep it, since it is what serializes the fibers inside a
  transaction. A permit is a scoped acquisition, and a statement's cost is dominated by how many Effect operations it
  runs.
- **Statement state.** A statement's state machine is one object with its methods on the prototype, rather than the
  seven closures plus a holder that a closure-based machine rebuilt per statement, and a query only builds the result
  shape its caller asked for. The garbage collector was the largest remaining cost on the query path; this halves its
  share of the concurrent run.
- **Row construction.** A `RowDescription` builds its row constructor once, and assignment stores the same property
  descriptor as `Object.defineProperty` an order of magnitude faster; only a `__proto__` column takes the slow
  spelling. `Object.defineProperty` was 18% of all samples in a CPU profile of the 100-row workload.
- **`PgProtocol.Parser.pushEach`.** `readField` was documented as settable from a `RowDescription`, but `push` finished
  the whole socket chunk first, so the reader never arrived before the rows it was meant to decode. Messages are now
  handed over as they are decoded, and a column costs neither a view over the parser buffer nor a second pass.
- **Prepared statements.** A repeated statement is kept under a backend name and costs `Bind`/`Execute`/`Sync` with no
  parsing, planning, or `RowDescription`. Per connection, keyed on SQL text plus inferred parameter OIDs, bounded by
  `preparedStatementCacheSize`, evicting least-recently-used and closing what it evicts. Recovers on its own from a
  name the backend has lost (`26000`) or a plan that no longer matches its columns (`0A000`). `prepare: false` opts
  out.
- **Pipelining.** A `multiplex` session writes the statements its fibers submit in the same tick as one batch and
  routes replies to the oldest cycle on the wire. Every cycle keeps its own `Sync`, so a rejected statement only skips
  its own cycle and nothing needs replay. Pinned work still owns the session, and `pin` waits for the pipeline to
  drain.
- **Spreading.** A multiplexed pool bounds how many statements share a connection. The backend runs a connection's
  pipelined statements in receipt order, so unlimited sharing meant the pool never opened a second connection and one
  slow statement held up everything in flight behind it. Bounding it costs no throughput and gains some.
- Frame tail and bind encoder built once instead of per statement, frames assembled in a pooled `Buffer`, a query
  assembling only the row shape its caller asked for, a pool checkout that only loops when a connection has to be
  replaced, and command tags split by reading their two spaces.

### Also in this PR

Two `Pool` liveness fixes, both found through this work:

- A lease was returned to the availability list only on the exact transition out of saturation, so several leases
  released together resumed one waiter and left the rest parked on an item that had room for them, with no later
  transition to wake them. This is what forced `PgPool` to give a multiplexed pool a concurrency of 2^20, and fixing
  it is what made bounded sharing possible.
- Invalidating an item that still had live leases removed it from circulation without topping the pool back up, so
  anybody already queued waited for an item that was never coming back.

And three in `sql-pg`:

- A statement the server refused to parse - a typo, a missing table - was treated as a fatal protocol error and
  destroyed the connection. The spec's fatal case is a failure of our own parser, not a SQL one. It is now an
  ordinary query error that fails only that statement.
- `stream` reaches a connection through the ordinary checkout and pins it itself, so a multiplexed pool kept handing
  the same connection out and a stream consumer running another statement could be given the connection its own
  stream was holding. Every route to an exclusive session goes through `PgConnection.pin`, so the reservation lives
  there now.
- `PgPool.invalidate` threw on a reserved connection: the pinned view copied its internals record from a base that
  had not assigned it yet.
- A connection dying while it was held left a queued checkout waiting forever, because the dead connection was only
  recorded for the *next* checkout to notice.

### Verified off Linux

Measured on an Apple M5 against the same `main` baseline, five interleaved pairs, PostgreSQL reached across an
OrbStack VM: one-row +5.7%, 100x3 +32.7%, 100x20 +50.6%, transaction +8.1%, 20 concurrent +10.3%. Two defects only
that environment could surface are fixed above - `noDelay` on the wrong socket, and the pool's borrow order.

### Tuning across a network

`multiplexConcurrency` sets how many statements share one connection. The default is low on purpose: pipelined
statements queue behind the slowest of them, and against a server a cheap round trip away, spreading over more
connections costs no throughput and buys tail latency. The further away the server, the more a round trip costs and
the more a deeper pipeline is worth - measured on macOS across an OrbStack VM, 32 was 21% faster than the default, and
16 was 7% faster even against a native server.

### Why `multiplex` is not the default

Pipelined statements execute in the order the backend received them, so sharing a connection trades tail latency for
throughput. With ten connections and a 500ms statement in flight, a non-multiplexed pool delays none of ten concurrent
fast statements; a multiplexed one delays three. Unbounded sharing delayed all ten, which is what the spreading change
fixes, but three is still not zero.

## Description

Lower the `@effect/atom-react` React peer dependency floor to 19.0.0 so the package supports every React 19 release, including React Native and Expo SDK versions pinned below the repository's test dependency.

The scheduler peer moves with it: React DOM 19.0 uses scheduler 0.25, React DOM 19.1 uses scheduler 0.26, and React DOM 19.2 uses scheduler 0.27. Keeping the scheduler floor at 0.27 would leave peer conflicts for React 19.0 and 19.1.

The package only uses React APIs available before React 19. React 18 support remains out of scope because its type definitions currently fail the package check and would need dedicated CI coverage.

tasks.title: Surface the provider's explanation on AuthenticationError
tasks.body:
## Type

- [ ] Refactor
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Bug Fix
- [ ] Optimization
- [ ] Documentation Update

## Description

`AiError.AuthenticationError` gets a new optional `description` field. It is shown after the kind-based suggestion, in the same way `InvalidRequestError` already shows its own description:

```
InvalidKey: Verify your API key is correct. invalid x-api-key (POST https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages?beta=true) [type: authentication_error]
```

Before this change, the message came only from `kind`. The provider's own 401/403 error text was thrown away, and the generic message could point the user in the wrong direction. The problem was found while using Amazon Bedrock (the Bedrock integration is a downstream project, not part of this repo). Bedrock returns HTTP 403 for several different problems: `ExpiredTokenException` ("The security token included in the request is expired") and `UnrecognizedClientException` ("The security token included in the request is invalid.") are credential problems, not permission problems. But both were shown as `InsufficientPermissions: Your API key lacks required permissions`. That message suggests fixing IAM policies, while the real fix was to refresh or correct a credential. The in-tree providers lose information in the same way: Anthropic's `invalid x-api-key`, OpenAI's `Incorrect API key provided: …`, and errors about organization/project scope or region restrictions were all reduced to the generic category. Because `description` is part of the core error type, downstream providers such as the Bedrock integration can pass their messages through in the same way.

All four providers (anthropic, openai, openai-compat, openrouter) now pass the provider message through on HTTP 401 and 403, exactly as they already did for `InvalidRequestError` at 400/404/422. The description also includes the request context, and the error type/code when the body cannot be parsed.

When `description` is absent, the rendered message is exactly the same as before, and `isRetryable` does not change. The provider-internal helper `buildInvalidRequestDescription` is renamed to `buildErrorDescription`, because it no longer serves only invalid-request errors.

## Validation

- `pnpm lint`
- `pnpm check`
- `pnpm vitest run packages/effect/test/unstable/ai/AiError.test.ts packages/ai/anthropic/test/AnthropicClient.test.ts packages/ai/openai/test/OpenAiClient.test.ts packages/ai/openai-compat/test/OpenAiClient.test.ts packages/ai/openrouter/test/OpenRouterClient.test.ts`

tasks.title: Fix MCP initialize rejected over the protocol version header
tasks.body:
<!--
Before submitting a Pull Request, please ensure you've done the following:

- 📖 Read our Contributing Guide: https://github.com/effect-ts/.github/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md
- 📖 Read our Code of Conduct: https://github.com/effect-ts/.github/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md
- 👷‍♀️ Create small PRs. In most cases this will be possible.
- 📝 Use descriptive commit messages.
- ✅ Provide tests for your changes if applicable.
- 📗 If your change requires documentation, please update the relevant documentation.
- 📝 Create a changeset for your changes. This helps in tracking and communicating the changes effectively.
- ⏳ Please be patient! We will do our best to review your pull request as soon as possible.

NOTE: Pull Requests from forked repositories will need to be reviewed by a team member before any CI builds will run.
-->

## Bug Fix

### Fix MCP initialize rejected over the protocol version header

`McpServer.layerHttp` validates the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header on every POST, including the `initialize` request. That header reports the version negotiated by an earlier `initialize`, so on a fresh connection a client can only send its own default. Whenever that default is not among the server's registered protocols, the `initialize` returns `400` and never reaches version negotiation, even when the body offers a version the server supports.

The `400` is also hard to diagnose, because the specification gives it a second meaning. Per [Streamable HTTP → Backwards Compatibility](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/transports#backwards-compatibility), a client that receives `400`, `404` or `405` from a POSTed `InitializeRequest` should conclude the endpoint speaks the deprecated two-endpoint HTTP+SSE transport and retry with a `GET`. `layerHttp` answers that `GET` with `405`, correctly, so the client discards the `400` and reports "this server does not support SSE transport" — true, and unrelated to the cause.

This scopes the header check to requests after initialization, where the specification requires it: the client "**MUST** include the `MCP-Protocol-Version` header on all **subsequent** requests", and its value "**SHOULD** be the one negotiated during initialization". An `initialize` now negotiates from the version offered in its body, through the protocol registry, which already falls back to the server's preferred protocol and reports the selection in the response header. Behavior after initialization is unchanged. Patch changeset included.

### Validation

Added `negotiates an initialize request from a client on an unsupported protocol version`: a server registering only `v2025_11_25` accepts an `initialize` from a client on `2025-06-18` and answers `200` with `mcp-protocol-version: 2025-11-25`. It fails against unpatched `main`.

All existing tests are green.

## Type

## Description

Enables outgoing message compression for WebSockets in `@effect/platform-bun`.

Although `perMessageDeflate` can be enabled on the Bun server since https://github.com/Effect-TS/effect/pull/6691, outgoing messages are still sent without Bun's compression flag. The test is rather complex because we need low-level access to the raw "wire data", since compression is fully abstracted away otherwise.

tasks.title: Add optional acquisition APIs to RcMap and LayerMap
tasks.body:
## Type

Feature

## Description

Adds `RcMap.getOption` with data-first and data-last overloads for atomically retaining an entry only when it is already cached. A missing key returns `Option.none` without invoking lookup or performing capacity acquisition. Existing ready or in-flight entries use the normal reference count and caller-scope finalizer, cached failures propagate unchanged, and closed maps interrupt.

This avoids the race inherent in composing `has` and `get`, where the entry can disappear between operations and `get` can start a new lookup.

Adds `LayerMap.contextEffectOption` as the direct optional counterpart to `contextEffect` on both `LayerMap` instances and generated `LayerMap.Service` classes. `Option.none` means the context is not currently cached on an open map, and missing entries do not build a layer.

The change does not modify existing release, TTL, invalidation, or capacity behavior. It includes API lifecycle coverage for missing entries, ready retention and release, in-flight sharing, cached failures, TTL retention and expiry, invalidation linearization, closed-map interruption, and direct and Service `LayerMap` accessors. It also includes an `effect` patch changeset.

Validation:

- 11 `RcMap` and `LayerMap` doctests passed
- `pnpm check`

tasks.title: feat: add `shouldTouch` option to `trigger()`
tasks.body:
## Summary

Adds a shouldTouch option to `trigger()`, mirroring the option that setValue already has. So callers can mark validated field(s) as touched without a setValue-based workaround.

### Motivation

`setValue` already supports `shouldTouch` to mark a field as touched, but `trigger()` has no equivalent. 
Anyone who wants to run validation and mark the validated field(s) as touched (e.g. validate-on-mount, multi-step form navigation, "show all errors on demand") currently has to reimplement this themselves by looping setValue(name, value, { shouldTouch: true }) over every field, which also re-writes values and triggers extra dirty/render work they don't actually want.

Maybe Related discussion
- https://github.com/react-hook-form/react-hook-form/discussions/9830

### What I have done

- Added `shouldTouch` to the `TriggerConfig` type.
- `trigger()` now marks the targeted field(s) as touched when shouldTouch: true is passed, following the same name / no-name scoping shouldFocus already uses:

```ts
trigger('name', { shouldTouch: true });          // marks `name` as touched
trigger(['a', 'b'], { shouldTouch: true });       // marks `a` and `b` as touched
trigger(undefined, { shouldTouch: true });        // marks every mounted field as touched
trigger('name');                                  // unchanged: no touched-state side effect
```

- Only `touchedFields` is written — `_formValues` is untouched, therefore there's no extra dirty-checking or value re-render cost compared to the setValue workaround.

### Test Plans

- Single field name marked as touched.
- Array of field names all marked as touched, others left untouched.
- No name (whole form) marks every mounted field as touched.
- Default behavior (no `shouldTouch`) stays a no-op for `touchedFields`, to guard against regressions.

### Test Results

```bash
Test Suites: 120 passed, 120 total
Tests:       1271 passed, 1271 total
Snapshots:   8 passed, 8 total
Time:        22.455 s
Ran all test suites in 2 projects.
=== tsc ===
TSC_OK
=== eslint ===
ESLINT_OK
=== DONE ===
```

tasks.title: fix(unregister): keepDirty inverted when broadcasting isDirty
tasks.body:
## Proposed Changes

`unregister`'s `keepDirty` option currently does the opposite of what it says, in both directions,
because the ternary that broadcasts `isDirty` carries its negation on the wrong side.

`createFormControl.ts:1584` reads:

```ts
_subjects.state.next({
  ..._formState,
  ...(!options.keepDirty ? {} : { isDirty: _getDirty() }),
});
```

so `isDirty` is recomputed **only when the caller asked to keep it**, and left stale when they did
not. The clearest symptom is on the option itself: `unregister('field', { keepDirty: true })`
correctly preserves `dirtyFields`, then recomputes `isDirty` and flips it to `false`. The option that
exists to preserve dirty state destroys half of it, and spends a `_getDirty()` pass to do so. On the
default path the inverse happens: `dirtyFields` is emptied at `:1568` while `isDirty` stays latched
at its previous value.

Every neighbouring line in the same block reads "unless the caller asked to keep it, clear or
recompute it":

```ts
!options.keepError && unset(_formState.errors, fieldName);
!options.keepDirty && unset(_formState.dirtyFields, fieldName);
!options.keepTouched && unset(_formState.touchedFields, fieldName);
...
!options.keepIsValid && _setValid();
```

`_reset` already spells the same option correctly at `:1962-1971`
(`keepStateOptions.keepDirty ? _formState.isDirty : <recompute>`). This one line is the odd one out,
and has been since the option was introduced.

The spread is the only thing that can refresh `isDirty` on this path: the emitted payload is merged
into `_formState` by `_setFormState`, and `useForm`'s resync effect depends on
`[control, formState.isDirty]`, so a value that never changes never retriggers it.

The fix deletes the negation, which makes `keepDirty` govern `isDirty` and `dirtyFields` identically
and makes `keepDirty: true` strictly cheaper than it is today, since it no longer runs `_getDirty()`.

**On the relationship to #13141 and #13162, which I looked at before opening this.** That discussion
was about `setValue(name, value, { shouldDirty: false })` leaving `dirtyFields` behind, and the
conclusion there was that keeping the two perfectly in step would mean recomputing on every
keystroke, which is not worth the cost. This change does not ask for that and adds no recomputation
at all: `_getDirty()` is already called on one of this ternary's two branches, and the fix only swaps
which branch gets it. The per-keystroke path is untouched. If the default-half of this is still
considered the documented trade-off, the `keepDirty: true` half stands on its own as a contract
violation and I am happy to narrow the change.

Two regression tests are added to `src/__tests__/useForm/unregister.test.tsx`, one per branch. Each
unmounts the input in the same click that unregisters it, so a still-mounted input cannot silently
re-register and mask the result. Against unpatched source they fail with `Expected: false, Received:
true` and `Expected: true, Received: false`; both `dirtyFields` assertions pass in that run, which is
what pins this as an `isDirty`-only inconsistency rather than a dirty-tracking failure.

tasks.title: fix: useWatch returns stale value on name change when new value is null
tasks.body:
### Problem
- useWatch's synchronous name/control-change fast path used null as a sentinel meaning "no immediate value computed yet," then fell back to the possibly-stale state value whenever the computed output was null.

### Root cause
- A watched field's actual value can legitimately be null (or a compute function can return null). When name changed to such a field, the sentinel collided with that legitimate value, so the hook returned the previous field's stale value for one render — until a layout effect corrected it on the next tick. 
- This breaks the documented guarantee that callers like `useController` see the correct value immediately on the same render.

### What I Fixed
- Replaced the sentinel with an explicit boolean flag (shouldReturnImmediate), so a genuinely null/undefined computed value is never mistaken for not computed yet.

### Testing
- Added a regression test that renders a component watching field a, then re-renders it watching field c (whose value is null), asserting the render triggered by the name change already returns null.
- Verified the test fails on the pre-fix code (Received: "x") and passes after the fix.

tasks.title: fix(setValues): update fields registered under an object or array value
tasks.body:
## Proposed Changes

`setValues` does not update a field that is registered at a path holding an object or an array. The input keeps its previous value even though `getValues()` reports the new one.

The batch loop flattens the incoming values and then matches mounted field names against the resulting keys:

```ts
const flattenedUpdates = flatten(updatedFormValues as FieldValues);

for (const fieldName of _names.mount) {
  if (fieldName in flattenedUpdates) {
    _setValue(fieldName, flattenedUpdates[fieldName], options, true, true);
  }
}
```

`flatten` only emits leaf paths, so `{ tags: ['b', 'c'] }` becomes `{ 'tags.0': 'b', 'tags.1': 'c' }`. A field registered as `tags` is never in that map, so `_setValue` is skipped and the element is left alone. An empty array or object is worse: it flattens to no keys at all, so the update disappears entirely.

In practice this hits the DOM controls whose value is an array under a single field name:

- `<select multiple {...register('tags')} />` keeps its old selection
- a checkbox group sharing one name keeps its old checked state
- a container path registered directly by a `Controller` never receives the new value
- `setValues({ tags: [] })` does not clear anything

`setValue('tags', ['b', 'c'])` handles all of these correctly today, so the two APIs disagree.

This replaces the flatten-and-lookup with a path walk over the provided values, so a container value is passed to `_setValue` as-is. `_setValue` already knows how to apply object and array values — it routes them through `setFieldValue`/`setFieldValues`, which handle multiple selects, checkbox groups and nested objects.

Path presence is resolved with own properties rather than `in`, which keeps two existing behaviours intact: an explicitly provided `undefined` still propagates to a mounted field, and a field name that collides with an inherited property (`toString`) is not treated as provided. The new `has` util mirrors `get`'s path semantics, including a path stored as a single literal key such as `{ 'a.b': 1 }`, so `has` and `get` agree on what is present.

`flatten` itself is unchanged and still used by `jsonToFormData`, where leaf-only output is what is wanted.

No linked issue — found while reading the `setValues` batch path.

### Tests

Three regression tests in `setValues.test.tsx` cover a multiple select, a checkbox group, and clearing a multiple select with `[]`. All three fail on `master`:

```
● setValues › should update a multiple select registered under an array value
    - Expected  - 2
    + Received  + 1
      Array [
    -   "b",
    -   "c",
    +   "a",
      ]

● setValues › should update a checkbox group registered under an array value
    expect(element).not.toBeChecked()
    Received element is checked:
      <input aria-label="a" name="choices" type="checkbox" value="a" />

● setValues › should clear a multiple select when an empty array is provided
    Expected length: 0
    Received length: 1
    Received object: [<option value="a">a</option>]

Tests: 3 failed, 18 passed, 21 total
```

`has` also gets its own unit test alongside the other `src/utils` tests.

tasks.title: fix(validateField): pass the field error to setCustomValidity when criteriaMode is all
✨ feat: add getErrors method to read form errors without subscription
tasks.body:
Hello, Bill 😁

Thank you for always responding and reviewing so quickly, even while you are busy with the v8 work.

I found the proposal in #12853 interesting, so I prepared a draft implementation of `getErrors`.

### Motivation

- Reads current errors on demand without adding a form-state subscription.
- Complements `setError` and `clearErrors` with familiar `getValues`-style call shapes.

I’m opening this PR as a draft and would appreciate your feedback on whether it aligns with RHF’s API direction and whether the proposed scope is appropriate.

### Situation

The existing ways to access errors in React Hook Form each have their own limitations.

`formState.errors` and `subscribe` are subscription-based, while `getFieldState` can only read one field at a time. Therefore, reading all errors on demand without subscribing currently requires accessing the private `control._formState.errors`.

### Proposal

I would like to propose a `getErrors` method with call shapes similar to `getValues`.

- `getErrors()` returns all currently stored errors.
- `getErrors(name)` returns the error for one field or error namespace.
- `getErrors(names)` returns multiple errors while preserving tuple order and length.

`getErrors` only reads the currently stored errors. It does not run validation or subscribe to form state.
